When I first read this in class I was instantly captured by this quote in the first chapter of the novel. Because it encapsulates one of the major themes in word for wordy: words. Language instead of being viewed as a way of bringing people together is viewed as a way of pushing them farther apart, of being competitive, of being used to evaluate people. Words in this novel hold power: there’s a competition for who can produce the most beautiful words, for who has the most succinct yet profound words, for who can make use of a word “just right”. 
On top of this power imbued in literacy, there is also a deep divide between people who have access to education and the luxuries it brings, and those who don’t have this access. The narrator Mira describes a game called Hippo, which is a made up game of “taking turns making words from a jig saw pile of Scrabble tiles” (Mufić 8). The goal is to choose tiles with the most points to form words which they would then define. This was a “privileged game” (Mufić 8), and one that Mira had to learn to play in order to interact and bond with her brother Harun who was “still in the stage of wanting his little sister to like him” (Mufić 8).
Although Mira knows how to play the game now, she didn’t use to, and so there was a “[s]ilence knotted in [her] throat” (Mufić 8) because she didn’t quite understand the rules, the pretension behind it, and the expectations placed upon her. Words and language in this game are almost like currency, the more impressive, rare or profound the word the more points the player gets, and so the more power and respect they gain from playing the game well. But if someone doesn’t understand the game, if someone doesn’t know how to play, they can’t participate in this exchange of gambling words for power. Thus, there is a divide created between the educated and the uneducated, the rich and the poor, even between siblings, by placing value in the way people use words in association to the strict rules of a game.

I picked up the book reluctantly, knowing from some downbeat reviews that it would not be a cheery read. The premise was intriguing, though — a teenage girl and her family try to build a new life in America after fleeing their war-torn country. An "American tenant farmer" has offered them a job picking strawberries. (Yes, I know there are no strawberries in upstate New York, but it's a fictional town.)As they work alongside other immigrants, both legal and illegal, Mira keeps wondering why the leaves change color — because that's what her late brother would have wanted her to explain to him. This becomes a metaphor for the questions she has about life in the new country, like why are some here legally and others not? "Leaves get their color from pigments," Mira began when Mom raised her eyebrows in expectation. "Chlorophyll is the most important one because it helps make food through photosynthesis. It's the reason leaves are usually green. But there are two other pigments in leaves: carotenoids and anthocyanins. Carotenoids are always present in leaves, but we can't see them when the leaves are green because the green color of the chlorophyll masks them. But when the days get shorter and the nights get longer in the fall, trees stop making chlorophyll. Then the green color of the leaves starts to fade away and the yellow and orange colors of the carotenoids can finally be seen. Anthocyanins are different because they are only produced in the fall. **Strengths:**

1. **Imaginative Elements:** The passage blends the mundane (writing a poem about cats) with the magical (paper glowing, a coat turning into an aurora). This juxtaposition immediately captures the reader’s curiosity and sets a whimsical, almost fantasy-like tone.

2. **Characterization:** Through Jonas’s actions and dialogue, the reader gains insight into his personality. He’s observant (“That’s new”) and slightly skeptical (“This isn’t my voice”). His mild confusion and discomfort feel authentic, making him relatable.

3. **Sensory Details:** Descriptions like the coat “turn[ing] into a bright purple aurora” and the “note… begin[ing] to glow golden” are vivid and engaging. These details help create a fantastical atmosphere.

4. **Internal Conflict:** The passage explores Jonas’s struggle between following the note’s request and expressing his own creative voice. This adds a subtle layer of tension and self-doubt.

1. **Clarity & Flow:** Some sentences are awkward or a bit redundant (“He unfolded it, and the note began to glow golden”). Combining ideas and tightening the prose would make the narrative smoother.
